title: Two Prayers and a Rich Man
sum: The journey to Jerusalem nears its end. Jesus tells two parables about prayer. A widow keeps demanding justice from a judge who fears neither God nor people until he gives in to be rid of her; how much more will God give justice to his chosen who cry to him day and night (18:1–8). A Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other people, while a tax collector stands far off and asks only for atonement, and it is the tax collector who goes home justified (18:9–14).

Here Luke rejoins Mark's order. Jesus welcomes babies, since the kingdom belongs to people like them (18:15–17). A rich leader who has kept the commandments is told to sell everything and follow; he grows sad, and Jesus says how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, though nothing is impossible with God (18:18–30). For the third time Jesus foretells his death and rising, and the Twelve understand none of it (18:31–34). Near Jericho a blind beggar calls him Son of David, receives his sight and follows him, praising God (18:35–43).
readings: Read as a chapter about who receives the kingdom

The widow with no power, the tax collector with no merit, the babies with nothing to offer and the blind beggar with no standing all receive; the righteous Pharisee and the law-keeping rich leader do not, or not yet. Read this way, the chapter is a single lesson on 18:17: the kingdom is received the way a child receives, as a gift.
Read as a chapter about prayer and faith

It begins with prayer that does not give up, and the question whether the Son of Man will find faith (18:8); it ends with a blind man whose faith saves him (18:42). Between them, two prayers in the temple show what kind of praying God hears.
Read with the Jewish setting in view

Every figure in the chapter is Jewish and every practice is Jewish piety: prayer at the hour of sacrifice, fasting, tithing, the commandments, the hope for David's son. Read this way, the chapter is an argument inside Israel about humility and mercy, not a contrast between Judaism and Christianity.

views.H: The parables draw on daily life: village and town courts where a widow without a male relative had little leverage; the temple's daily sacrifices, morning and afternoon, when people gathered to pray; voluntary fasts on Mondays and Thursdays; tithes on every purchase. Jericho was a wealthy oasis on the pilgrim road from Perea, with Herodian palaces and plenty of tolls to collect.
views.C: The two prayer parables (18:1–14) are Luke's special material, found in no other Gospel; with 18:15 Luke rejoins Mark (Mark 10:13–52), having left Mark's order at 9:50. He passes over Mark's debate on divorce (Mark 10:1–12, though he has the saying at Luke 16:18) and the request of James and John (Mark 10:35–45; compare Luke 22:24–27). He shortens and smooths Mark's Greek, as Cadbury showed, and puts the healing at the approach to Jericho to make room for Zacchaeus.
views.L: Luke pairs a woman and a man (the widow, the Pharisee and tax collector), as he often does. The chapter is built on reversals: the persistent widow, the justified sinner, the babies who are welcome, the rich man who cannot let go, the blind man who sees while the Twelve do not understand (18:34). "Justice" (18:3–8) and "justified" (18:14) tie the two parables together.
views.J: Jewish readers note that the Pharisee's prayer of thanks has parallels in Jewish prayer, that his fasting and tithing were admirable, and that "God, be gracious to me, the sinner" is itself the voice of the Psalms (Psalm 51; Psalm 25:11). Amy-Jill Levine argues that the parable's original hearers might have been shocked that the tax collector was justified "rather than" the Pharisee, and suggests the Greek par' ekeinon could even mean the tax collector was justified "because of" the Pharisee, whose merit benefits the community, a reading few scholars follow. The widow's cry echoes Sirach 32.
views.T: The tax collector's prayer became the root of the Orthodox Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner"), and the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee opens the Orthodox Lenten Triodion. The Catechism of the Catholic Church cites the parable to teach that humility is the foundation of prayer (2559, 2613). Luther and the Reformers read 18:14 as a picture of justification by faith. The call to sell everything, in its parallel form (Matthew 19:21), sent Antony of Egypt into the desert and helped begin Christian monasticism (Athanasius, Life of Antony 2).

deep.b:
Luke's two parables are built as a pair. Both are about prayer, both use the language of justice (ekdikēsis, 18:3–8; dedikaiōmenos, 18:14), and both end with a judgment Jesus speaks in the first person: "I tell you" (18:8, 14). In the first, the widow's persistence wins justice from a bad judge, and Jesus argues from the lesser to the greater: God is not like that judge. In the second, the man who trusts his own righteousness gains nothing, and the man who asks for atonement goes home right with God.

Christian preaching has often made the Pharisee a symbol of Judaism and the tax collector of the church, or the Pharisee of "religion" and the tax collector of "grace." Both caricatures distort the parable. The Pharisee's fasting and tithing were real devotion, and Jewish prayer did thank God for one's lot (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 28b). The parable's target is named in 18:9: trusting in oneself and despising others, a temptation of religious people in every tradition, including Luke's own church (16:15). As many interpreters, Levine among them, point out, a reader who thanks God that he is not like that Pharisee has become him.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the justice the widow asked for
deep.b: The word family of 18:3–8 (ekdikeō, ekdikēsis, "give justice") appears in Luke only here and once more, in 21:22, where the fall of Jerusalem is called "days of ekdikēsis." Between the two, Luke sets the widow who is devoured (20:47) and the widow who gives her whole living (21:1–4). I suggest that Luke means these passages to be read together: the cry of God's chosen for justice (18:7) is answered, but justice in Luke cuts both ways. The same "days" that vindicate the oppressed fall on the city whose leaders "eat up widows' houses." Read this way, the parable's question "will he find faith?" (18:8) is not only about the end of the world but about Jerusalem's coming crisis, which the disciples must survive by holding out (21:19). Commentators note both passages, but I have not seen this verbal link argued as a deliberate frame.

settings.what: The parable of the widow and the judge
settings.to: his disciples (17:22), on the road to Jerusalem
settings.when: right after his teaching on the sudden days of the Son of Man (17:22–37)
settings.why: To keep his followers praying and trusting while they wait for God to set things right. A widow wins her case even from a judge who cares nothing for justice; God, who is just and loves his chosen, will act for them. The closing question turns it into a test of the hearers: will the Son of Man find this kind of faith?
settings.readers: Luke's readers, a generation or more later, lived with delay and with pressure from outside. The parable told them that God's justice was certain and that their task was to keep praying.
views: Most read it as encouragement: God is the opposite of the judge and will vindicate his people.
Many have read it as a lesson in persistent prayer, like the friend at midnight (11:5–8).
A minority (Herzog) reads it as a picture of a widow shaming a corrupt court, with no figure for God.

settings.what: The parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector
settings.to: "some people" who were sure of their own righteousness and looked down on others (18:9)
settings.when: on the journey to Jerusalem, after the parable of the widow
settings.why: To overturn the hearers' sense of who stands right with God. The man everyone would call righteous goes home without God's approval; the one everyone would call a sinner goes home justified. The point is not that devotion is bad, but that trusting in it and despising others shuts a person out of God's mercy.
settings.readers: For Luke's mixed church, the parable warned against new kinds of contempt, of Gentile Christians for Jews or of the respectable for the newly converted.
views: Some take "some people" to be Pharisees, as in 16:14–15.
Others note that Luke does not say so and that the warning reaches anyone, the disciples included.

settings.what: Jesus blesses the babies
settings.to: the disciples who were turning parents away, with the parents present
settings.when: on the road, as people brought infants for him to touch
settings.why: To correct the disciples, who thought babies not worth the teacher's time, and to teach that the kingdom is received by those who have nothing to bring.
settings.readers: Luke's readers would have heard it in a church that baptized households (Acts 16:15, 33) and debated who belongs.

settings.what: The rich leader and the cost of following
settings.by: Jesus, with a leader and then Peter
settings.to: a wealthy leader, then all who were listening, then Peter and the disciples
settings.when: on the road toward Jericho
settings.why: To show the leader the one thing standing between him and eternal life, his wealth; to warn the listeners how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom; and to assure the disciples who had left everything that God would repay them many times over.
settings.readers: Luke's Gospel is the one most concerned with wealth and the poor; his readers included well-off householders who supported the church (8:3; Acts 16:14–15), and this story asked them what their property meant to them.

settings.what: The third prediction of the passion
settings.to: the Twelve, taken aside
settings.when: as they near Jerusalem
settings.why: To prepare the Twelve for what was coming and to tell them it fulfills the prophets. They could not grasp it, and Luke says the meaning was hidden until the risen Jesus would explain it (24:44–46).

settings.what: The blind man's cry and Jesus' answer
settings.to: Jesus, over the heads of the crowd
settings.when: on the road into Jericho
settings.why: The beggar calls on Jesus by the royal title Son of David and will not be silenced. Jesus' words, "See again. Your faith has saved you," give him sight and make him a follower.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the man who sees and follows is a picture of discipleship, in contrast with the Twelve who "could not grasp" (18:34).

traditions.q: The tax collector goes home "justified" from the temple after one plea for atonement, with no baptism, no sacrament and no good work to show (18:14). Is he a model of justification by faith alone, of the contrite repentance the church's sacraments continue, or a case before the cross that does not settle the later debate? (For what justification itself means, see the card at Genesis 15:6.)
views: The tax collector shows the disposition that prepares for justification: faith in God's mercy, fear of judgment and sorrow for sin, which the Council of Trent lists as the steps by which grace moves a sinner (Session 6, chapter 6). The Catechism cites the parable to teach that humility is the foundation of prayer (2559, 2613), and his words have long been used as a prayer of contrition. That he was justified without a sacrament does not set the sacraments aside: the Catechism teaches that contrition arising from love of God obtains forgiveness even of grave sins when it includes the resolve to go to confession as soon as possible (1452).

The scene is read less as a legal verdict than as the pattern of repentance (metanoia) that the whole Christian life repeats. The tax collector's prayer is the root of the Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner"), and the Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee opens the Lenten Triodion, so that the church enters Lent with his words. Humility, not a single moment of verdict, is what the parable teaches.

The parable is a picture of justification by faith alone: the Pharisee brings his works and goes home unjustified; the tax collector brings nothing but his sin and his trust in God's mercy, and is declared righteous. His plea is faith, not a work that earns the verdict. That the scene is set before the cross does not matter to this reading, since the same God justified Abraham by faith (Romans 4).

Reformed readers agree that the tax collector is justified freely, apart from works, and see the Pharisee as every attempt to stand on one's own righteousness. They also stress that his justification rests on the atonement he asks for (hilasthēti, "be propitiated"), which is fulfilled in Christ's sacrifice, which is credited to the one who believes (Westminster Confession 11.1).

title: The King Comes to His City
sum: In Jericho the chief tax collector Zacchaeus, too short to see over the crowd, climbs a fig tree. Jesus calls him down and invites himself to his house. The crowd grumbles, Zacchaeus pledges half his goods to the poor and fourfold repayment to anyone he cheated, and Jesus declares that salvation has come to the house of this son of Abraham, for the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost (19:1–10).

Because they think the kingdom is about to appear, Jesus tells of a nobleman who goes to a far country to receive a kingdom; his citizens send envoys to reject him, his slaves are tested with a mina each, and on his return the faithful are rewarded, the timid slave loses his mina, and the enemies are slain (19:11–27). Jesus rides a colt down the Mount of Olives while his disciples hail him as the King who comes in the Lord's name (19:28–40). He weeps over Jerusalem, foretelling its siege and destruction because it did not recognize God's visit (19:41–44). He drives the sellers out of the temple and teaches there daily, while the leaders look for a way to destroy him (19:45–48).
readings: Read as the end of the journey

Luke's long journey (9:51–19:44) ends here. It ends with a rich man saved, a parable of a king who must go away before he reigns, a royal welcome by disciples, and tears over a city that will not receive him. Read this way, the chapter sums up the journey's themes: the lost found, the kingdom delayed, the king rejected.
Read politically

A nobleman seeking a crown from a distant emperor, citizens who reject him, a royal entry on a colt, a temple seized for a day: every scene of the chapter is about kingship. Luke's King comes in peace (19:38, 42), on a borrowed colt, without branches or Hosannas, and weeps over his city instead of conquering it.
Read as a chapter of visitation

Zacchaeus receives Jesus' visit with joy (19:6); Jerusalem does not recognize "the season when you were visited" (19:44). Read this way, the chapter sets the right and wrong responses to God's coming side by side.

views.H: Jericho was a rich toll town with Herodian palaces. The parable of the minas fits the story of Archelaus, who went to Rome in 4 BC to be confirmed as king and was opposed by an embassy of fifty Jews (Josephus, Antiquities 17.299–314). The siege Jesus describes in 19:43–44 matches what Titus' army did in AD 70: ramps, then a wall around the city, then the leveling of its buildings (Josephus, War 5–7).
views.C: Zacchaeus (19:1–10) and the lament over Jerusalem (19:41–44) are Luke's alone. The parable of the minas shares a core with Matthew's talents (Matthew 25:14–30), which most assign to the source called Q, with a throne-claimant story woven in. Luke's entry follows Mark 11:1–10 but drops the Hosannas and the branches, adds "King" and the Pharisees' protest, and shortens the temple scene to two verses. Many date Luke after AD 70 partly because of 19:43–44; others argue it echoes the Old Testament's sieges.
views.L: Luke closes the journey with a chiasm of welcome and rejection: Zacchaeus welcomes Jesus with joy, the citizens reject their king, the disciples welcome him as king, Jerusalem fails to recognize him. "Today" (19:5, 9) and "peace" (19:38, 42) are keywords. Jesus' tears (19:41) answer the disciples' joy (19:37).
views.J: Zacchaeus is restored as "a son of Abraham" (19:9), a Jewish insider, not a Gentile convert. His fourfold repayment goes beyond what the Torah requires. Jewish readers note that Jesus' lament over Jerusalem stands in the line of Jeremiah's and of later Jewish laments for the temple, and that Christian readings of 19:41–44 as God's final rejection of the Jews ignore the grief in it.
views.T: Zacchaeus' story is read in the Roman Catholic rite for the dedication of a church, because Jesus says "Today salvation has come to this household." In the Orthodox calendar the Sunday of Zacchaeus marks the approach of the Lenten season. Palm Sunday celebrates the entry, though Luke's account has no palms. The "Benedictus qui venit" of the Mass ("Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord") draws on 19:38 and its parallels.

deep.b:
Luke's parable of the minas (19:11–27) and Matthew's parable of the talents (Matthew 25:14–30) share a plot: a master entrusts money to slaves, goes away, returns, rewards two who traded, and condemns one who kept the money safe out of fear; his words "everyone who has something will be given more" end both. The differences are large. Matthew's master gives five, two and one talents, huge sums, "to each according to what he could handle"; Luke's nobleman gives ten slaves one mina each, a modest sum. Matthew's reward is charge over much and the master's joy (Matthew 25:21, 23); Luke's is rule over a set number of towns. Only Luke has the throne-claimant who goes to receive a kingdom, the citizens' embassy and the slaughter of enemies.

Most scholars think the two go back to one parable, which each Gospel shaped for its readers. Matthew sets it among the parables of readiness for Christ's return (Matthew 24–25), told on the Mount of Olives; Luke sets it at Jericho, to correct those who thought the kingdom would appear at once (19:11). Others think Jesus told similar stories on different occasions, as teachers do. Luke's added strand about the rejected king makes the parable a preview of the next week: the king will be rejected by his own city (19:14; 23:18–21) and will return in power (21:27).

deep.h: Jesus' tears and the city's fall
deep.b:
Luke has four passages on Jerusalem's fate: the lament "Jerusalem, Jerusalem" (13:34–35), the weeping over the city (19:41–44), the discourse on its siege (21:20–24) and the words to the women on the road to the cross (23:27–31). All four are in a tone of grief, not triumph. They stand in the tradition of Israel's own prophets: Jeremiah wept for his people and warned that the temple would be destroyed (Jeremiah 7:14; 9:1), and the book of Lamentations mourns the fall of 587 BC.

Christian writers from the second century on often treated the city's fall in AD 70 as God's verdict on the Jews for rejecting Jesus, a theme that fed centuries of hostility. Luke's text does not draw that conclusion. Jesus weeps; he gives the reason as failure to recognize "what leads to peace"; the judgment has a limit (21:24); and in Acts the gospel goes "to the Jew first," with thousands of Jerusalem's people believing (Acts 2:41; 21:20). On the larger question see the anti-Judaism and church-and-Israel topics.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a gallery of givers
deep.b: Between 18:18 and 21:4 Luke sets one person after another beside their money. The rich leader will give nothing and grows sad (18:23). Zacchaeus gives half, and repays fourfold (19:8). The slaves in the parable put their master's money to work, and one hides it (19:13–24). The scribes devour widows' houses (20:47). The poor widow gives everything (21:4). The order does not rise step by step: it is a series of contrasts, and I suggest Luke arranged it so that it ends where it began, at the two poles. "Sell everything you have" (18:22) is not done by the man who could, and is done by the woman who had almost nothing, just before Jesus speaks of the temple's end. Scholars have long noted Luke's interest in possessions (the classic study is Luke Timothy Johnson, The Literary Function of Possessions in Luke-Acts, 1977), but I have not seen this framing of these chapters argued.

echoes: Ezekiel 34:11–16; Exodus 22:1; Leviticus 6:5; 2 Samuel 12:6; Matthew 25:14–30; Mark 11:1–19; Matthew 21:1–17; John 12:12–19; Zechariah 9:9; 1 Kings 1:33–40; 2 Kings 9:13; Psalm 118:26; 2:14; 13:34–35; Habakkuk 2:11; Isaiah 29:3; Psalm 137:9; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; 1:68; 7:16; 21:20–24; 23:27–31

settings.what: Zacchaeus and Jesus' declaration of salvation
settings.to: Zacchaeus, with the grumbling crowd listening
settings.when: in Jericho, the last town before Jerusalem
settings.why: Jesus calls a despised chief tax collector by name and invites himself to his house; Zacchaeus answers with a public pledge of generosity and restitution. Jesus' words "Today salvation has come to this household" are spoken to Zacchaeus but aimed at the crowd: they restore him as a son of Abraham and explain Jesus' mission to find the lost.
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, Zacchaeus showed that a rich man can be saved (18:27) and what salvation does to money.

settings.what: The parable of the ten minas
settings.to: the crowd at Zacchaeus' house and on the road, who thought the kingdom was about to appear (19:11)
settings.when: at Jericho, about 25 kilometers from Jerusalem, a few days before Passover
settings.why: To correct the expectation that Jesus would take power as soon as he reached Jerusalem. The king must go away to receive his kingdom; his servants must be faithful with what he has given them while he is away; and those who refuse his rule face judgment.
settings.readers: Luke's readers lived in the time of the king's absence and still faced opponents. The parable told them to be faithful and to expect his return as king.
views: Matthew's talents (Matthew 25:14–30) is told privately to the disciples on the Mount of Olives, about readiness for Christ's return; Luke's minas is told publicly at Jericho, about the delay of the kingdom.
Most read the nobleman as Christ; some (Herzog, Schottroff) read him as a portrait of a cruel earthly king like Archelaus, with the third slave as a resister.

settings.what: The disciples' acclamation and Jesus' reply to the Pharisees
settings.by: the crowd of disciples; then Jesus
settings.to: God, in praise; then Pharisees in the crowd
settings.when: on the road down the Mount of Olives toward the city
settings.why: The disciples greet Jesus with Psalm 118, sung by pilgrims at the festivals, and add "King." The Pharisees, perhaps fearing the Romans' reaction to a royal claim, want it stopped; Jesus answers that the praise cannot be silenced.
settings.readers: Luke's readers knew the outcome: the King hailed here would be crucified under the title "King of the Jews" (23:38).

settings.what: Jesus' lament and prophecy over Jerusalem
settings.to: the city of Jerusalem, addressed as a person, with the disciples hearing
settings.when: as he first catches sight of the city from the Mount of Olives
settings.why: To grieve over a city that was missing the moment of God's visit, and to warn, as the prophets had, of siege and destruction to come.
settings.readers: Readers who knew of the city's fall in AD 70 (whenever Luke wrote, his readers soon did) heard it as a word fulfilled, and as Jesus' grief rather than his triumph.
views: Many read it as a genuine prediction in the prophets' siege language.
Others think Luke shaped it in the light of AD 70.

settings.what: Jesus' word in the temple
settings.to: the sellers in the temple courts, with the people present
settings.when: on entering the temple
settings.why: To reclaim the temple as a house of prayer, quoting Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, and to make room for his daily teaching there.
views: Mark sets the clearing on the day after the entry, framed by the cursing of the fig tree (Mark 11:11–21); Matthew, like Luke, puts it on the day of arrival (Matthew 21:12–13). Luke's account is the shortest of the three. John places a temple clearing at the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2:13–22).

title: Questions in the Temple Courts
sum: As Jesus teaches in the temple, the chief priests, scribes and elders demand to know by what authority he acts. He asks them whether John's baptism was from heaven or from people; afraid of the crowd, they say they do not know, and he refuses to answer them (20:1–8). He tells the people a parable of tenants who beat the owner's slaves and kill his beloved son; the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others, and the rejected stone will crush whoever opposes it. The leaders know the parable is aimed at them (20:9–19).

Spies posing as honest men ask whether to pay tribute to Caesar, hoping to deliver him to the governor; Jesus answers, "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (20:20–26). Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose the riddle of a woman married to seven brothers; Jesus answers that the children of the resurrection neither marry nor die, and that God is the God of the living (20:27–40). He asks how the Messiah can be David's son when David calls him Lord (20:41–44), and warns his disciples against scribes who seek honor and devour widows' houses (20:45–47).
readings: Read as a trial before the trial

Every group that will condemn Jesus questions him here: the chief priests, scribes and elders (20:1), spies who aim to bring him before the governor (20:20), the Sadducees of the high priest's party (20:27). Read this way, the chapter is a preliminary hearing in which the accused wins every exchange, so that the real trial (22:66–23:25) can only proceed by false charges (23:2).
Read as Jesus' teaching on the great questions

Authority, Israel's history with God, the state, life after death, the Messiah's identity, and the abuse of religion. Read this way, the chapter is Luke's summary of Jesus' public teaching in Jerusalem.

views.H: Tenant farming for absentee landlords was common in Judea and Galilee. Tribute to Rome had been a flash point since Judas the Galilean's revolt in AD 6. The silver denarius of Tiberius bore his portrait and called him son of the divine Augustus. The Sadducees, the high-priestly party, accepted only the written Torah and denied the resurrection; the Pharisees affirmed it.
views.C: Luke follows Mark 11:27–12:44 closely, with changes: he names the people as the audience of the tenants parable, adds "for a long time" and "perhaps," leaves out most of Isaiah 5, adds the crushing stone (20:18), names the governor as the spies' goal, replaces Mark's "head tax" with "tribute," expands the resurrection answer with the two ages (20:34–36) and "for to him all are alive" (20:38), and omits the great commandment, which he told in 10:25–28.
views.L: The chapter is framed by the people (ho laos), who listen to Jesus (20:1, 45) and whom the leaders fear (20:6, 19, 26). Luke repeats that the leaders cannot "seize on" what he says (20:20, 26). The beloved son of the parable (20:13) is the Son the heavenly voice named (3:22), and the rejected stone (20:17) returns in Peter's speech to the same leaders (Acts 4:11).
views.J: Every debate here is an argument among Jews about Jewish questions: the source of a prophet's authority, Israel as God's vineyard, the legitimacy of tribute to a pagan emperor, the resurrection (which the Pharisees and later rabbis defended from the Torah, as Jesus does), and the meaning of a psalm. Luke notes that some scribes approved Jesus' answer (20:39). The parable of the tenants is aimed at the leaders, who "could tell he had aimed this parable at them" (20:19), not at the people, who are horrified at its ending (20:16).
views.T: "Render to Caesar" has been the starting point of Christian teaching on church and state (see the card on Matthew 22). The resurrection debate is cited in Catholic and Orthodox teaching on consecrated celibacy as a sign of the age to come ("neither take wives nor are given as wives"). Psalm 110:1 became central to the creeds' confession that Christ "sits at the right hand of the Father."

deep.h: Luke's changes to the temple debates
deep.b:
Luke's chapter follows Mark's order, but its changes show his interests. First, the audience: Luke says the tenants parable was told "to the people" (20:9), and that the leaders feared "the people" (20:19). The people are on Jesus' side until the trial. Second, Rome: Luke says the spies meant to deliver Jesus "to the governor's rule and authority" (20:20), and later reports the false charge that he forbade tribute (23:2). Luke's readers, in the Roman world, would see that Jesus was no rebel. Third, the resurrection: Luke adds that the risen are "children of God, being children of the resurrection" and that "to him all are alive" (20:36, 38), and leaves out Mark's rebuke "You have gone far astray" (Mark 12:27). Fourth, the scribes: Luke lets some scribes approve (20:39) and moves the friendly scribe's question about the first commandment to an earlier chapter (10:25–28).

For the background of each debate (authority, the vineyard, Caesar's coin, the Sadducees and levirate marriage, David's son), see the notes and deep dives on Mark 11:27–12:40 and Matthew 21:23–22:46.

echoes: Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 8:14–15; Daniel 2:34–35; Daniel 2:44–45; Acts 4:11; Romans 13:6–7; Deuteronomy 25:5–6; Exodus 3:6; Exodus 3:15; 4 Maccabees 7:19; Daniel 12:2–3; Psalm 110:1; Acts 2:34–35; Mark 11:27–12:40; Matthew 21:23–22:46; 23:2

settings.what: The question of authority
settings.by: Jesus, with the chief priests, scribes and elders
settings.to: the temple leaders who challenged him, in front of the people
settings.when: one day during his teaching in the temple, after he had cleared the sellers
settings.why: The leaders demand his credentials; Jesus answers with a question about John's baptism, which shows that they had already refused God's messenger and were afraid of the people. He does not owe them an answer.

settings.what: The parable of the tenants
settings.to: the people, with the scribes and chief priests listening (20:9, 19)
settings.when: in the temple courts, right after the leaders' challenge
settings.why: To answer the question of authority with a story: the owner has sent servant after servant, and now his beloved son, and the tenants will be judged. It warns the leaders that rejecting the son will cost them the vineyard, and tells the people that the rejected stone will be vindicated.
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw the history of the prophets and of Jesus, and in Acts the same leaders confronted with the rejected stone (Acts 4:11).
views: Mark and Matthew aim the parable at the chief priests, scribes and elders who had just challenged him (Mark 11:27; 12:1, 12; Matthew 21:23, 33, 45); Luke has Jesus tell it to the people, with the leaders overhearing and seeing that it was about them (20:9, 19).
Luke says the leaders knew it was aimed at them; most scholars read it as a warning to the temple authorities.
Many Christian readers took it as God's rejection of the Jews; the card at Matthew 21:43 sets out the churches' views.

settings.what: Tribute to Caesar
settings.by: Jesus and spies sent by the leaders
settings.to: the spies, before the people
settings.when: in the temple courts
settings.why: The question was a trap: either answer could ruin him, with the people or with the governor. Jesus' answer gives Caesar his coin and claims for God what bears God's image, and leaves the trappers nothing to report.

settings.what: The Sadducees' question about the resurrection
settings.to: Sadducees, with scribes and the people listening
settings.when: in the temple courts
settings.why: The Sadducees ridicule the resurrection with an absurd case drawn from the levirate law. Jesus answers that the age to come is unlike this one, and proves the resurrection from the Torah they accept: God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and to him all are alive.

settings.what: Whose son is the Messiah?
settings.to: those around him in the temple, including the scribes
settings.when: after his questioners had fallen silent
settings.why: To show from Psalm 110 that the Messiah is more than David's son: he is David's Lord. Luke's readers would hear the answer in Peter's first sermon (Acts 2:34–36).

settings.what: Warning against the scribes
settings.to: his disciples, with all the people listening
settings.when: in the temple courts
settings.why: To warn the future leaders of his community against the love of honor and the exploitation of the weak that he saw in some religious leaders, and to warn that such leaders face a harsher judgment.
settings.readers: For the leaders of Luke's churches the warning was about themselves (22:24–27).
views: Matthew expands this short warning into a long speech of woes against the scribes and Pharisees, spoken to the crowds and the disciples (Matthew 23); Luke, like Mark (Mark 12:38–40), keeps it brief, having given his own woes at a Pharisee's table (11:37–54).

title: Not One Stone on Another
sum: Jesus sees rich people putting gifts into the temple treasury and a poor widow dropping in two tiny coins, and says she has given more than all of them: she gave her whole living (21:1–4). When some admire the temple's beautiful stones and gifts, he says that not one stone will be left on another (21:5–6). Asked when this will happen, he warns them not to follow those who claim his name or say the time has come. Wars, earthquakes, famines, plagues and signs from heaven will come, but before all that his followers will be persecuted, handed over to synagogues and prisons, and brought before kings and governors; he will give them words no opponent can answer, and by holding out they will win their lives (21:7–19).

When Jerusalem is surrounded by armies, its desolation is near: those in Judea must flee, for these are days of retribution; the people will fall by the sword and be taken captive, and Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (21:20–24). Then there will be signs in the sun, moon and stars and terror among the nations, and the Son of Man will come in a cloud with power and much glory; his followers are to lift their heads, for their redemption is near (21:25–28). The fig tree teaches them to read the signs (21:29–33). They must stay alert and pray, so as not to be caught like a trapped bird (21:34–36). Jesus teaches in the temple by day and spends the nights on the Mount of Olives (21:37–38).
readings: Read as two events, carefully separated

Luke's discourse distinguishes the fall of Jerusalem (21:20–24), described in plain historical terms, from the coming of the Son of Man (21:25–28), which follows "the times of the Gentiles." Read this way, Luke has already answered a question that Mark and Matthew leave open: the temple's fall is not the end of the world.
Read as a word for a persecuted church

Much of the discourse is about the disciples: persecution, trials before kings and governors, betrayal by family, the promise of words and wisdom, endurance, alertness and prayer. Read this way, it is pastoral more than predictive, and Acts shows it lived out.
Read with the four classic views

Preterist readers see almost all of it fulfilled in AD 66–70; futurist readers, in events still to come; others, a near and a far fulfillment. The four-views table in the deep dives on Matthew 24 applies here too.

views.H: Herod's temple, rebuilt from about 20 BC and still being finished in the 60s, was famous for its size and beauty. In AD 66 the Jewish revolt against Rome broke out; in AD 70 Titus surrounded Jerusalem, built a siege wall, and took and burned the city and the temple. Josephus records the dead and the 97,000 captives. Later Christian writers said the Jerusalem church fled to Pella before the siege.
views.C: Luke rewrites Mark 13. He sets the scene in the temple, narrows the disciples' question to the temple, adds warnings against those who say "the time has drawn near," places persecution "ahead of" the signs, replaces "the abomination of desolation" with Jerusalem surrounded by armies, adds the captivity and "the times of the Gentiles," and ends with a call to prayer instead of Mark's parable of the doorkeeper. Many date Luke after AD 70 because of 21:20–24; others reply that the language comes from the Old Testament's sieges (see the deep dive).
views.L: The discourse moves from the temple (21:5–6) to the persecuted church (21:12–19), to Jerusalem (21:20–24), to the whole world (21:25–26, 35), and ends at the Son of Man (21:27, 36). "Days will come" (21:6) is answered by "that day" (21:34). The chapter is framed by two pictures of people in the temple: the widow giving all (21:1–4) and the people coming at dawn to hear (21:38).
views.J: The destruction of the Second Temple is mourned in Judaism every year on Tisha b'Av, together with the fall of the First Temple. Jewish scholars read Jesus' words as those of a Jewish prophet warning his people, like Jeremiah; they stress that "wrath on this people" (21:23) has been misused to blame the Jews for their own suffering, and that "until" (21:24) implies the judgment is not final.
views.T: Luke's "times of the Gentiles" became central to dispensational prophecy, especially after 1967. Catholic teaching connects the end with the recognition of the Messiah by "all Israel" (Catechism 674). The church fathers, such as Eusebius, read 21:20–24 as fulfilled in AD 70, and the flight to Pella as obedience to 21:21. Advent liturgies in many churches read 21:25–36 as the first Sunday's Gospel in Luke's year.

deep.h: Did Luke write after the fall of Jerusalem?
deep.b:
Where Mark wrote "when you see 'the abomination of desolation' standing where he must not stand" (Mark 13:14), Luke wrote "when you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps" (21:20), and added that the people would fall by the sword, be carried off captive, and Jerusalem be trampled (21:24). Many scholars take this as the clearest sign that Luke wrote after AD 70: he has replaced Mark's riddle with what actually happened. Combined with Luke's use of Mark and his sense of a long time before the end (21:9, 24), this places Luke, in most accounts, around 80–90.

Others reply that nothing in Luke's description goes beyond what the Old Testament said of earlier sieges, such as Babylon's in 587 BC: armies around the city (Isaiah 29:3; Ezekiel 4:1–3), the sword and captivity (Deuteronomy 28:64; Jeremiah 21:7), "trampled" (Zechariah 12:3). C. H. Dodd argued in 1947 that Luke's oracles were composed from this Old Testament language, not from AD 70; Bo Reicke and John A. T. Robinson argued that Luke-Acts was written before 70, noting that Acts ends with Paul alive in Rome about AD 62 and never mentions the city's fall. Luke also says nothing of the temple's burning, the famine or the factional fighting that Josephus describes. The question is open; the majority view is a date after 70, and the minority view has serious defenders.

deep.h: What Luke adds to Mark 13 and Matthew 24
deep.b:
The deep dives on Matthew 24 ("Ways to read the discourse," "Matthew, Mark and Luke") and Mark 13 ("What Mark adds to Matthew 24") cover the discourse as a whole. Luke's own contributions are these: the warning against those who say "the time has drawn near" (21:8) and the words "first" and "not right away" (21:9); persecution set "ahead of all these things" (21:12), as Acts would show; Jesus himself giving "a mouth and wisdom" (21:15); "not one hair from your head will be lost" and "win your lives" (21:18–19); the siege, the captivity and "the times of the Gentiles" (21:20–24); the roaring sea and the nations' dread (21:25–26); the singular cloud of Acts 1:9–11 (21:27); "stand tall and raise your heads" (21:28); "every tree" (21:29); and the closing call to sobriety, alertness and prayer, ending with standing before the Son of Man (21:34–36).

Luke leaves out Mark's saying that no one knows the day or hour, "and the Son does not know" (Mark 13:32), the shortening of the days for the chosen (Mark 13:20), and the false messiahs' signs (Mark 13:21–23), some of which he has used in 17:22–37.

echoes: Mark 12:41–13:37; Matthew 24:1–36; 17:20–37; 19:41–44; Daniel 7:13–14; Daniel 9:26–27; Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 34:4; Isaiah 24:17; Hosea 9:7; Zechariah 12:3; Deuteronomy 28:64; Micah 7:6; Exodus 4:12; Romans 11:25–26; Acts 1:9–11; Acts 6:10; 1 Thessalonians 5:1–8; Revelation 11:2

settings.what: The widow's offering
settings.to: his disciples and those around him in the temple courts
settings.when: by the offering chests, just after warning against scribes who devour widows' houses
settings.why: To show that God measures a gift by what it costs the giver, and, in context, to expose a system that took a poor widow's last coins.

settings.what: The discourse on the temple's fall and the coming of the Son of Man
settings.to: people admiring the temple (21:5), who then ask him when it will happen (21:7); the discourse addresses Jesus' followers (21:12–19), with the people listening (20:45; 21:38). In Luke it is spoken in the temple courts, not on the Mount of Olives
settings.when: during the last days of teaching in the temple, before Passover
settings.why: To answer the question about the temple's fall, warn against deceivers and against expecting the end at once, prepare the disciples for persecution, tell them when to flee Jerusalem, and lift their eyes to the Son of Man's coming and their own redemption.
settings.readers: Luke's readers, after AD 70 if Luke wrote then, as most scholars think, would know of the temple's fall; all of them knew the church's persecution and were still waiting for the Son of Man.
views: Mark and Matthew place it on the Mount of Olives, with four or all of the disciples; Luke keeps it in the temple, with a wider audience.
Preterist, futurist and two-stage readings are set out in the deep dives on Matthew 24.

settings.what: Warnings and the coming persecution
settings.to: the disciples
settings.when: within the discourse
settings.why: To keep them from being misled by false claims and frightened by wars and disasters, and to strengthen them for trials before synagogues, prisons, kings and governors.
settings.readers: Acts records these very trials, which Luke's readers would recognize: Peter and John, Stephen, James, Paul before Felix, Festus and Agrippa.

settings.what: The prophecy of Jerusalem's siege
settings.to: the disciples, and through them those living in Judea
settings.when: within the discourse
settings.why: To tell them to flee, not to hold out in the city, when the armies come; to declare the siege a time of judgment foretold by the prophets; and to set a limit: "until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled."
settings.readers: For readers after 70, the words were fulfilled; for all readers, the "until" raised the question of what comes after (see the card).

settings.what: The coming of the Son of Man
settings.to: the disciples
settings.when: within the discourse
settings.why: To describe the end in the prophets' images of cosmic upheaval and to tell his followers that, when others faint with fear, they should stand up straight: the Son of Man's coming is their redemption.

settings.what: The parable of the fig tree
settings.to: the disciples
settings.when: within the discourse
settings.why: To teach them to read the signs as they would read spring leaves, and to assure them that his words will outlast heaven and earth.

settings.what: The call to watchfulness and prayer
settings.to: the disciples
settings.when: the end of the discourse
settings.why: To warn that hangovers and everyday worries are as dangerous as persecution, because the day will come suddenly, and to call them to constant alertness and prayer so they can stand before the Son of Man.
settings.readers: For Luke's comfortable readers, the danger was less persecution than distraction.

traditions.q: Jerusalem will be "trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (21:24). Does that "until" promise a future for Jerusalem and the Jewish people when those times end? (Whether the church has replaced Israel is the card at Matthew 21:43.)
views: Yes. The "times of the Gentiles" is the long period of Gentile world power over Jerusalem, from Nebuchadnezzar to Christ's return, after which God will restore Israel and Christ will reign from Jerusalem. Many dispensationalists saw Israel's capture of the Old City in 1967 as a sign that those times were nearing their end.

The Catechism teaches that Christ's glorious coming is held back until he is recognized by "all Israel," citing Romans 11:20–26 (Catechism 674); many Catholic interpreters read the "until" of this verse in that light. The church does not attach this to any modern political event.

Most Reformed interpreters read the times of the Gentiles as the whole age of the gospel going to the nations, with no promise of an earthly restoration of Jerusalem. Many also expect, from Romans 11, a large turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end, but within the one church.

Progressive dispensationalists and many historic premillennialists hold that "until" implies a real future for Israel as a people, fulfilled when Christ returns, while rejecting date-setting from current events.
